newsitem.title: BARBADOS: Clinton says no decision on Latam arms sales.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says no decision on Latam arms sales.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Saturday he had still not decided whether to relax a virtual ban on weapons sales to Latin America, but expressed concern that other countries might corner the market.
"On that, I can tell you that no decision has been made yet," Clinton, visiting Barbados for a summit with Caribbean leaders, told a questioner at a news conference.

He was commenting on an open letter addressed to him while he was visiting Costa Rica earlier this week by Oscar Arias, former president of that country and a Nobel Peace laureate. The letter urged Clinton to promote arms control in the region.
"The United States will not knowingly do anything that will spark a new arms race or divert funds from non-defence to defence areas in Latin America," Clinton said.

"The real question is whether or not the armies in question ... are going to upgrade their militaries anyway, and whether it would be better in fending off future conflicts and controlling defence spending for the United States, the hemispheric partner, to be the main supplier, or someone else."
Clinton said the United States had no interest in selling the arms for purely economic reasons.
In his letter, published in the Costa Rican daily La Nacion, Arias said:

"It's time that the voices of our boys and girls are heard clamouring for schools and not for arms. And it's time that the arms dealers read the diaries written in our jails by those who suffered torture and mutilation at the hands of our military."

Current U.S. policy, dating back to the Cold War era when many Latin American countries were run by dictators, calls for restraint in sales of high-tech weaponry although it allows requests to be reviewed on a case-by-case basis.

The advent of democracy in the continent has prompted a review of the policy, and U.S. officials said in January that then secretaries of state and defence, Warren Christopher and William Perry, had suggested easing the restrictions.
The issue is politically sensitive, however, because of the past history of repression in Latin American countries, the still-persisting feuds between some of them, and the high poverty rates there.

The Clinton administration broke new ground in March by allowing U.S. aircraft manufacturers to submit bids to Chile for the purchase of fighter jets, but U.S. officials insisted this did not change the "case-by-case" policy.
Clinton said on Saturday that he was still trying to make a judgment on the issue and had so far received no final recommendation from "my administration top personnel."
Jamaican Prime Minister P.J. Patterson told the news conference that his country and other Caribbean states endorsed Arias' appeal.
